pamphlet_excerpts: Person-First Language: Many people with disabilities want to emphasize what they areable to do rather than emphasize their disabilities (p. 9).
Person-First Language Principle 2: Remember that people with disabilities are people first (p. 9).
Person-First Language Principle 3: Each person gets to decide how he or she should be described (p. 9).
Person-First Language Principle 4: You should useperson-first language when talking about people who are notpersonal acquaintances or about people with disabilities as agroup (p. 9).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Person-First Language): When you make a new friend or talk about an individual, show a person-first attitude by calling the individual what he orshe wants to be called (p. 9).
Step 2 (Person-First Language): Many people with disabilities see their condition as part ofwho they are, just like their gender, hair or eye color, or ethnicity (p. 9).
Step 3 (Person-First Language): Writing and talking with person-first language is a goodhabit to get into because it is the proper form for most situations (p. 9).
Step 4 (Person-First Language): Don't call someone an epileptic when you mean to saythe person has epilepsy (p. 9).

requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Talk with a Scout who has a disability and learn about the Scout's experiences taking part in Scouting activities and earning different merit badges. Discuss what you have learned with your counselor. (b) Talk with an individual who has a disability and learn about this person's experiences and the activities in which this person likes to participate. Discuss what you have learned with your counselor. (c) Learn how people with disabilities take part in a particular adaptive sport or recreational activity. Discuss what you have learned with your counselor. (d) Learn about independent living aids such as service animals, canes, and augmentative communication devices such as captioned telephones and videophones. Discuss with your counselor how people use such aids. (e) Plan or participate in an activity that helps others understand what a person with a visible or invisible disability experiences. Discuss what you have learned with your counselor.

Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: Maybe you belong to a club for people who share your interest, such as an astronomy club or a collectors' group (p. 19).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: Youmight have a friend from the club who has a disability (p. 19).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: Talk with your friend about his or her experiences (p. 19).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Find outwhat adaptations or adjustments, if any, your friend has madeor used to take part in favorite activities or do everyday tasks (p. 19).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Talk with a Scout who has a disability and learn about the Scout's experiences in Scouting (p. 19).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Have any badges presented especially difficult or unsolvable problems (p. 19).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Find out about any adaptive gearor techniques the Scout may have used to achieve Scoutinggoals (p. 19).
